414.title: Why worry, mind
414.hook: kaahe re man chitveh udam: why plot and scheme, mind, when even creatures in the rocks are fed (Gujri M5, ang 10)
414.howItsDone: Kaahe re man chitveh udam is the fifth shabad of Rehras Sahib, recited each evening; Sikhs pair its trust in the Lord's provision with kirat karni, earning an honest living.

segments.voice: Yesterday, binau, and your line, the humble ask. Did you ask someone for help? Today, the fifth shabad of Rehras, the second in Raag Gujri, and it speaks straight to a worried mind. Day four hundred fourteen.

Two in the morning. The house is dark and everyone else is asleep, but your mind is wide awake and running scenarios. What if the job falls through. What if the test results are bad. What if I say the wrong thing tomorrow. You plan, re-plan, rehearse arguments that haven't happened. None of it changes anything at two a.m. Guru Arjan knew that mind. And he wrote it a shabad that starts with a question. Today: why worry.
screen: `2 A.M. EVERYONE ELSE ASLEEP.` → `WHAT IF, WHAT IF, WHAT IF.` → `A SHABAD FOR THE WORRIED MIND.`

segments.voice: It opens: kaahe re man chitveh udam. Why, mind, do you plot and scheme, when the dear Lord Himself has taken care of your keeping? Then the picture that gives us today's line. In rocks and stones, the shabad says in paraphrase, He created living beings, and He places their food in front of them. Think of a tiny creature living in a crack in a rock, nowhere near a field or a market, and still it's fed. Then the refrain: whoever meets the true congregation is carried across, and by the Guru's grace, even dry wood turns green. Then a harder line. Mother, father, friends, children, spouse: no one, finally, is anyone's support. The Lord provides for each and every head, so why are you afraid, mind? And another picture. A bird flies hundreds of kos, the old measure of distance, leaving its young behind. Some translators make it a crane. Who feeds them? Who teaches them to peck? They remember her, the shabad says. It closes: all treasures and powers lie in the palm of the Lord's hand; Nanak is forever a sacrifice; You have no limit. Does this mean don't work, don't plan? No. Sikh life is built on kirat karni, honest work, and elsewhere gurbani praises effort. The word here is about the anxious scheming of a mind that thinks everything depends on it alone. Do your work. Then put the two a.m. worry down. Even the rock-creatures eat.
screen: `KAAHE RE MAN: WHY SCHEME, MIND?` · `IN THE ROCKS, FOOD PLACED BEFORE THEM.` · `A BIRD FLIES FAR; WHO FEEDS THE YOUNG?` · `WORK HONESTLY; PUT THE WORRY DOWN.` · then, large: `EVEN THE ROCK-CREATURES EAT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: put one worry down. Name one worry that's been riding with you. Hold it in your mind as if it were a stone in your hand. Feel how heavy it is. Ask: is there one honest thing I can do about this today? If yes, note it. Then picture setting the stone down on the ground beside you. It's still there. You're just not carrying it for the next two minutes. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once, and let the hand stay open. The bell holds the time.
Why worry. Kaahe re man chitveh udam: Guru Arjan asks the anxious mind why it schemes, when even creatures in the rocks are given their food.
Your line: even the rock-creatures eat. Tonight, if worry wakes you, do the one honest thing you can, or note it for morning, then set the stone down. Day four hundred fourteen.

415.title: Chaupai at nightfall
415.hook: the Benti Chaupai, now prayed as darkness comes
415.howItsDone: In Rehras Sahib, after the nine shabads, Sikhs recite Guru Gobind Singh's Benti Chaupai, followed by a savaiya and a dohra; it is also one of the morning banis, and many Sikhs say it before a journey or at night.

segments.voice: Yesterday, why worry, and your line, even the rock-creatures eat. Did you set one stone down? The nine shabads of Rehras are done. Now comes a prayer you already know, in a new light. Day four hundred fifteen.

Last thing at night, in a lot of houses, someone does the rounds. Back door locked. Stove knob checked, twice. A glance through the curtain at the street. A child's door pushed open an inch, just to hear the breathing. Nobody calls it a prayer. But it's one of the oldest things a household does: before the dark, make sure everyone is inside and kept. And the night still finds other ways in: a hospital ward, an empty flat, a long drive home. Today: Chaupai.
screen: `LAST THING AT NIGHT: THE ROUNDS.` → `EVERYONE INSIDE AND KEPT.` → `THE NIGHT STILL FINDS WAYS IN.`

segments.voice: After the nine shabads, Rehras moves from the Guru Granth Sahib to the Tenth Guru's words: the Benti Chaupai of Guru Gobind Singh, the same prayer many Sikhs said this morning. You spent ten days with it earlier on this path, so you know its first lines. In paraphrase: protect me, giving me your hand. May the wish of my heart be fulfilled. May my mind stay at your feet. Take me as your own, and look after me. In the morning, those words go out with you into the day. In Rehras, they're said as the light is going, and they land differently. Shelter is what you ask for at dusk. Whoever does the rounds at night isn't looking for adventure. They want the door shut, a lamp on, someone keeping watch. That's the posture of the Chaupai in Rehras. And it isn't a frightened prayer. It was written by a Guru who faced real armies and real nights, and it never pretends danger isn't there. It simply asks, in the middle of it, to be kept. Right after it, Rehras carries the short savaiya and dohra you met at the close of that block: since I took hold of your feet, I look to no one else; leaving every other door, I've come to yours. So the order is a shape. Shelter me with your hand. I've stopped knocking on other doors. Yours is the one I'm at as night comes. Shelter for the night.
screen: `FROM THE NINE SHABADS TO THE TENTH GURU.` · `GIVE ME YOUR HAND AND KEEP ME.` · `AT DUSK, WHAT YOU ASK FOR IS SHELTER.` · `EVERY OTHER DOOR LEFT; YOURS AT NIGHT.` · then, large: `SHELTER FOR THE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read two lines at dusk. If you have the Chaupai on your phone or in a gutka, find the first two lines and read them slowly, aloud or under your breath: hamree karo haath dai rachhaa, pooran hoe chit kee ichhaa. If not, hold their meaning: protect me, giving me your hand; may the wish of my heart be fulfilled. Then picture the coming night: where you'll sleep, who's near, what you're carrying into it. Let the lines rest over it like a roof. The bell holds the time.
Chaupai, Guru Gobind Singh's Benti Chaupai, said in the morning and again inside Rehras as darkness comes: protect me, giving me your hand.
Your line: shelter for the night. Tonight, before you lock the door or turn out the light, say the first line of the Chaupai, or its meaning, once. Day four hundred fifteen.

416.title: Anand at nightfall
416.hook: the six ceremony pauris close the day in joy
416.howItsDone: In Rehras Sahib, the Benti Chaupai and its savaiya and dohra are followed by six pauris of the Anand, then the Mundavani and a slok by Guru Arjan, the passages that also close the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chaupai, and your line, shelter for the night. Did you say its first line before the lights went out? Today, what comes after the shelter, as Rehras nears its end. Day four hundred sixteen.

A long day. You walk in, drop your bag, and before you've even sat down, someone puts a plate in front of you. Hot dal, a roti folded on the side, maybe a little achaar. You didn't ask. It's just there. Nobody makes a speech about it. You just sit. Safe first, then fed. That's the order the evening prayer follows too. Yesterday, the shelter. Today, the plate. Today: Anand.
screen: `A LONG DAY. A PLATE PUT DOWN.` → `YOU DIDN'T ASK. IT'S JUST THERE.` → `SAFE FIRST, THEN FED.`

segments.voice: After the Chaupai asks for shelter, Rehras turns to joy: the six pauris of the Anand, the first five and the fortieth. You know them now. Anand bhaiaa meree maae: joy has come, my mother. And at the very end, anad sunahu vaddabhaageeho: hear the bliss, you fortunate ones. Notice the order inside Rehras. First, protect me. Then, joy has come. Fear is spoken to before joy is sung. And the joy isn't a reward for a good day. It's just what the night is given. Then, after the Anand, Rehras closes with two short passages that also come at the very end of the Guru Granth Sahib. The first is called the Mundavani, often explained as the seal, and it has a dinner-table picture of its own. In paraphrase, by Guru Arjan: on this plate, three things have been placed: truth, contentment and contemplation. The nectar of the Name is set there too, the support of all. Whoever eats it, whoever enjoys it, is saved. The second is a slok, also by Guru Arjan, a short, grateful confession. In paraphrase: I didn't appreciate what You did for me; You made me worthy. I have no virtue; You took pity on me, and I met the True Guru, my friend. So the evening prayer ends at a table. Shelter, then joy, then a plate with truth, contentment and reflection on it, and a thank you for what you didn't earn. Joy at dusk.
screen: `AFTER SHELTER, THE SIX PAURIS OF JOY.` · `PROTECT ME, THEN JOY HAS COME.` · `MUNDAVANI: A PLATE OF TRUTH, CONTENTMENT.` · `SLOK: YOU MADE ME WORTHY.` · then, large: `JOY AT DUSK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hum anand bhaiaa. Sit back, as if you've just come home and the plate is in front of you. Hum, or softly say, anand bhaiaa meree maae, satguroo mai paaiaa. Joy has come, my mother; I have found the True Guru. Hum it two or three times, as slowly as you like. Then picture the plate: truth, contentment, a moment of reflection. Take one thing from it for tonight. Rest there. The bell holds the time.
Anand, joy: in Rehras, after the Chaupai's plea for shelter, the six pauris of the Anand bring joy, and the Mundavani sets a plate of truth, contentment and contemplation.
Your line: joy at dusk. Tonight, at dinner, before the first bite, notice the plate, and hum anand bhaiaa once, even silently. Day four hundred sixteen.

417.title: Ardas at day's end
417.hook: many families close Rehras standing together in Ardas
417.howItsDone: Sikh families often stand together for Ardas after Rehras, hands folded, one person leading and all saying Waheguru at set points; it ends with Nanak naam chardhi kalaa, tere bhaane sarbat daa bhalaa.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anand, and your line, joy at dusk. Did you notice the plate at dinner? Rehras has ended. Now, in some homes, everyone stands up. Day four hundred seventeen.

A front room in the evening. The last line of Rehras has been said. A grandmother puts her hands together and gets up from the sofa, a little slowly. The teenager looks up from her phone, sighs, and stands too. Somebody turns the TV off. The youngest boy stands on the cushion so he's taller. Nobody announces it. Everyone just knows: this is the part where we stand. Today: Ardas.
screen: `THE LAST LINE OF REHRAS.` → `A GRANDMOTHER STANDS; THEN EVERYONE.` → `THIS IS THE PART WHERE WE STAND.`

segments.voice: Ardas is the Sikh standing prayer. Tradition traces the word to a Persian phrase for a petition, the kind of written request a subject would bring to a ruler. Sikhs say it standing, hands folded, often facing the Guru Granth Sahib if one is in the house. One person leads; the others listen, and say Waheguru together at certain points. It isn't a shabad from the Guru Granth Sahib. It's the community's own prayer, with a standard form set out in the Sikh code of conduct. It opens by remembering: the ten Gurus by name, then the Guru Granth Sahib. Then the long line of Sikhs who kept faith, who served, who suffered and gave their lives, are brought to mind. Then comes the asking, for the whole community and for the world. And there's a place where a family can name tonight's particular reason: a grandfather in hospital, a new baby, an exam tomorrow, a safe journey. Then the close, in its set words: Nanak naam chardhi kalaa, tere bhaane sarbat daa bhalaa. In paraphrase: through Nanak's Name, may spirits rise; by Your will, may all be well. Not may we be well. May all be well. So the family in the front room ends the day by standing up for everyone, and naming the one or two people on their mind. Then the Sikh greeting: Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh. Then they sit back down. Stand at day's end.
screen: `ARDAS: A PETITION, SAID STANDING.` · `REMEMBER: THE GURUS, THE SIKHS WHO KEPT FAITH.` · `NAME TONIGHT'S REASON.` · `SARBAT DAA BHALAA: MAY ALL BE WELL.` · then, large: `STAND AT DAY'S END.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand for one minute's prayer. If you can, stand up now, feet steady, hands together in front of you. If you can't stand, sit up straight; that's fine. Bring to mind the people who carried you here: parents, teachers, anyone who kept faith before you. Then name one person on your mind tonight. If you pray, you can hold them before God in the plain words of your heart, or say Waheguru. Then widen it, the way Ardas does: may all be well. Stay there. The bell holds the time.
Ardas, the Sikh standing prayer that closes Rehras in many homes: remembering the Gurus and the faithful, naming tonight's need, and asking that all be well.
Your line: stand at day's end. Tonight, before bed, stand for a moment, think of one person, and widen it to everyone. Day four hundred seventeen.

418.title: Dusk as a practice
418.hook: lamps lit, work put down, the family gathered
418.howItsDone: Sikhs say Rehras Sahib in the evening, after sunset, and some households mark dusk by putting work down, lighting a lamp and gathering, though the remembrance, not the lamp, is the heart of it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ardas, and your line, stand at day's end. Did you stand for a moment and widen it to everyone? Today, not a text, but a time of day. Day four hundred eighteen.

Your phone probably knows when the sun sets. Around dusk the screen goes a little warmer, a little dimmer, without you asking. Somebody decided our devices should notice the evening. It's easy not to. A day can go straight from the last meeting to the commute to dinner to scrolling in bed, and never quite end; it just runs out. Long before screens, Punjabi households had a way to make the evening a real turning point. Today: dusk as a practice.
screen: `YOUR PHONE NOTICES SUNSET.` → `IT'S EASY NOT TO.` → `THE DAY DOESN'T END; IT RUNS OUT.`

segments.voice: The old Punjabi word is sandhiaa. It comes from a root meaning a joining: the seam where day and night meet. In South Asia, households of more than one faith mark that seam. Lamps are lit. Shoes come off. Work is put down. Hindu neighbors keep sandhya prayers too, and in Punjabi homes, Sikh and Hindu, a small lamp at dusk has been an ordinary sight. For Sikhs, dusk is when Rehras is said. The Sikh code of conduct places it in the evening, after sunset. Notice how that's put. Not to the minute. In the evening, as the light goes. The Gurus questioned rituals kept for their own sake, and gurbani puts remembrance above outward observance. So the lamp isn't the prayer. It's a reminder that the prayer is due. What makes dusk a practice, then, is the putting down. The shop shutter comes down. The laptop closes. The family, or just you, gathers. The day is handed back. Sikh life asks for kirat karni, honest work, through the day, and sandhiaa is the moment that work is allowed to stop. That's the gift of a seam. Without it, today bleeds into tonight and tonight into tomorrow, and nothing is ever finished. With it, the day can actually end. Put the day down.
screen: `SANDHIAA: THE SEAM OF DAY AND NIGHT.` · `LAMPS LIT, SHOES OFF, WORK DOWN.` · `REHRAS IN THE EVENING, AFTER SUNSET.` · `THE LAMP REMINDS; REMEMBRANCE PRAYS.` · then, large: `PUT THE DAY DOWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: light one lamp at dusk. If you can, light a candle or a small lamp now, or just switch on one warm light and turn off the overhead. If it isn't dusk yet, plan where you'll do it tonight. Look at the light. Then name, silently, one piece of today's work you are putting down: the email, the argument, the unfinished task. Picture setting it on a shelf till morning. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once, and let that be the evening beginning. The bell holds the time.
Sandhiaa. Dusk, the joining of day and night, when Sikhs say Rehras: lamps lit, work put down, the household gathered.
Your line: put the day down. Tonight, choose one moment, a shutter, a closed laptop, a lit lamp, that says the workday is over, and keep it. Day four hundred eighteen.

419.title: Rehras with others
419.hook: a household that prays Rehras together hears the day end the same way
419.howItsDone: Rehras Sahib is recited in the evening in gurdwaras with the sangat, and families often say it together at home, one person often leading, ending with Ardas said standing; some families now join by phone or video across cities.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sandhiaa, dusk as a practice, and your line, put the day down. Did you keep one moment that ended the workday? Today, the same evening prayer, said with other people. Day four hundred nineteen.

Seven-thirty in the evening, a small house in Birmingham. A father props his phone against the fruit bowl. On the screen: his sister in Toronto, still at her kitchen counter in the afternoon light, and her two kids squeezed into the frame. He starts: so dar keha. His sister joins on the second line. The kids murmur, then catch up by the Chaupai. Two cities, two clocks, one Rehras. Today: sangat.
screen: `A PHONE PROPPED ON THE FRUIT BOWL.` → `BIRMINGHAM AND TORONTO, ONE SCREEN.` → `TWO CLOCKS, ONE REHRAS.`

segments.voice: Rehras can be said alone, on a train, under your breath. It's also said together: a household in the front room, a congregation in the gurdwara in the evening, cousins on a video call across continents. Why does that matter? Gurbani puts a lot of weight on sangat, the company of people who remember the One. Guru Nanak asks, in Sri Raag, how the true congregation is to be recognized, and answers, in paraphrase: it's where the One Name is spoken. Not where the building is grandest. Where the Name is. You've heard this all through Rehras. Guru Nanak, stuck in the mud, sought the shelter of those who remember. Guru Arjan said join the company of the holy, and that whoever meets the true congregation is carried across. Rehras keeps pointing at other people. There's also something simpler. When a household says Rehras together, the children hear it before they can read it. They learn where the pauses fall, which lines the grandmother says slowly, when everyone stands for Ardas. A day that ends the same way for everyone in a house gives the house a shared clock. Even when the day went badly, even after an argument at dinner, everyone hears the same words: joy has come, mother; protect me with your hand; may all be well. Saying it together doesn't erase the argument. But it's hard to stay quite as far apart after you've stood side by side for Ardas. End the day together.
screen: `ALONE, OR TOGETHER: HOME, GURDWARA, SCREEN.` · `SANGAT: WHERE THE ONE NAME IS SPOKEN.` · `REHRAS KEEPS POINTING AT OTHER PEOPLE.` · `A HOUSE WITH A SHARED CLOCK.` · then, large: `END THE DAY TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: invite one person to join. Think of someone you could end a day with: a partner, a child, a parent, a friend who lives far away. It doesn't have to be the whole of Rehras. It might be two lines of the Chaupai, or one minute of quiet together, or just a shared thank you. Picture asking them. Picture what it would be like to end tonight side by side, even by phone. Hold that picture and breathe. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once, for them. The bell holds the time.
Sangat, the congregation: the evening prayer said together, at home, in the gurdwara or across a screen, so a household and a sangat hear the day end the same way.
Your line: end the day together. Tonight, ask one person to share one minute with you at day's end: a line, a quiet, a thank you. Day four hundred nineteen.

420.title: Rehras close
420.hook: morning Japji, evening Rehras: the day is held at both ends
420.howItsDone: Sikh nitnem frames the day: the Japji and other banis in the morning, Rehras Sahib in the evening when work is done, and Kirtan Sohila at night before sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sangat, and your line, end the day together. Did you share a minute with someone at day's end? Today we close Rehras, on our sixteenth day with it. Day four hundred twenty.

Look at a shelf of books. Take away one bookend, and the row starts to lean. Take away both, and the books slide over in a heap. Put a bookend back on each side, and the whole row stands up straight, every book in its place, even the thin ones in the middle. Nothing in the middle has changed. It's just held at both ends. That's the shape of the Sikh daily prayers. Today: nitnem.
screen: `A SHELF OF BOOKS.` → `NO BOOKENDS: THE ROW SLIDES.` → `HELD AT BOTH ENDS, IT STANDS.`

segments.voice: Sikhs call the daily prayers nitnem, the daily rule. In the morning, the Japji of Guru Nanak and the other morning banis. In the evening, Rehras. And at night, as we'll see tomorrow, Kirtan Sohila. Two bookends and a nightlight. Look back at what we packed for the road. Rehras opened at the door: so dar, what is that door, where everything sings. Hearsay calls You great; only one who has seen can say. Saying it I live, forgetting I die. Then So Purakh, that Being without stain. Kartaa, the river everything flows in. The pool of fire and water, feet stuck in the mud, and a hand from those who remember. Maanukh. A humble plea, with the word rahraas hidden inside. Why worry, mind, when even the rock-creatures eat? Then the Tenth Guru's Chaupai: shelter for the night. The Anand's joy, and a plate of truth, contentment and contemplation. Ardas, standing, asking that all be well. Dusk itself, sandhiaa, as a practice. And the prayer said together. So what is Rehras for? The morning Japji sends a person out into the day. Rehras gathers them back in, with the same Name and many of the same Gurus. The hours in the middle, the thin books on the shelf, the commute, the meetings, the dishes, stand up straight because they're held from both sides. Both ends held.
screen: `NITNEM: THE DAILY RULE.` · `THE DOOR, HEARSAY, REMEMBERING, SO PURAKH.` · `THE MUD, YOUR CHANCE, THE PLEA, WHY WORRY.` · `CHAUPAI, ANAND, ARDAS, DUSK, TOGETHER.` · then, large: `BOTH ENDS HELD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: set a bookend at each end of today. Think of this morning. Was there a beginning, any beginning: a line, a breath, a moment before the phone? If there was, remember it. If not, that's fine. Now think of tonight. Choose your bookend: a line of Rehras, the first line of the Chaupai, the Anand's joy has come, or just a minute of quiet before sleep. Decide it now, and decide tomorrow morning's too. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once, for both. The bell holds the time.
Nitnem, the daily rule: sixteen days with the Sikh evening prayer, nine shabads, the Chaupai, the Anand, the Mundavani and Ardas, holding the day's far end as the Japji holds its start.
Your line: both ends held. Today, keep one bookend at each end of the day, however small. Tomorrow, the night song. Day four hundred twenty.

original.note: Gurmukhi: nitnem, the daily rule; the set prayers that frame the Sikh day, morning, evening and night.

trapdoor: what you thought: Rehras is just the evening version of morning prayers.
what it means: its own prayer, packed for the road, that gathers the day back in as the Japji sent it out.

what a scholar hears: Rehras gathers five Gurus' voices, Guru Nanak, Guru Amar Das, Guru Ram Das, Guru Arjan and Guru Gobind Singh, and ends with passages that come at the close of the Guru Granth Sahib.
